title: Ship working code while you sleep with the Ralph Wiggum technique
summary: Matt Pocock demos Ralph Wiggum (credited to Geoffrey Huntley's article), a deliberately primitive orchestration technique for coding agents: a bash for loop that invokes Claude Code over and over against a task list until everything is done. He explains why it beats both parallel agent swarms (merge conflicts, hidden dependencies) and elaborate multi-phase markdown plans (painful to re-plan, doesn't match how engineers actually pull work off a kanban board). The implementation is ralph.sh, run with a max-iteration cap, which feeds the agent two files: prd.json (user stories with passes flags, doubling as product requirements and to-do list) and progress.txt (an append-only memory log for the sprint). Each iteration picks the single highest-priority feature, implements it, runs pnpm typecheck and pnpm test, marks the PRD item passing, appends progress notes, and makes a git commit; the loop exits early when the agent prints a PROMPT_COMPLETE sentinel, and a small TypeScript CLI pings him on WhatsApp when finished. He shows a human-in-the-loop variant (ralph-once.sh) running one interactive iteration with Opus 4.5, and closes with the investment thesis: stronger feedback loops - types, tests, browser MCP - are what make Ralph produce working code instead of endless slop.
what_you_learn: You get a complete, copyable architecture for unattended agent coding: the loop script, the PRD-as-todo-list file format, the append-only progress log, the one-feature-per-iteration discipline, and the feedback loops (typecheck, tests, CI green) that keep each commit honest. It reframes orchestration from framework building to process design - the orchestrator is a for loop plus file conventions, and the human's job shifts from planner to requirements author.

learnings.title: Ralph is a for loop, not an orchestration framework
learnings.detail: The dream of agentic coding is waking up to working code from your backlog. Instead of agent swarms, meshes, and orchestrators, Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph Wiggum article (July 14) advocates the simplest possible approach: a bash loop that gives the LLM a list of tasks and runs it again and again until complete. It only works because the underlying coding models (Opus 4.5, GPT 5.2) are now good enough that simpler approaches are viable - and often better than complex ones.

learnings.title: Why swarms fail and single-context agents break
learnings.detail: Running 16 parallel agents on 16 tasks is hellish: merge conflicts everywhere and hidden dependencies between tasks that are hard to spot. One agent doing everything is also impossible: the tasks collectively overflow a single context window, the LLM gets confused, and output quality craters. Ralph threads the needle - one agent, many fresh context windows, one task per iteration.

learnings.title: Multi-phase markdown plans are brittle; kanban loops are not
learnings.detail: The common alternative is an LLM-authored multi-phase plan (built in Claude Code plan mode) executed phase by phase. Matt's complaint: inserting a new task means manually reworking arrows and ordering, which doesn't reflect how engineers work - they pull the next highest-priority task off a board. With a kanban-style loop you only design the end state; adding work means appending a specification, nothing else changes.

learnings.title: ralph.sh takes a max-iterations cap and guards errors
learnings.detail: The script starts with set -e style error handling, requires a max-iterations argument (it yells at you if you omit it), then runs a for loop bounded by that cap so a runaway LLM cannot loop forever. Each iteration logs its number, invokes a CLI coding agent (Claude Code, opencode, codex - any CLI-invokable agent works), and checks the output for a completion sentinel. A separate tiny TypeScript notify CLI sends a WhatsApp message when it finishes after X iterations.

learnings.title: prd.json is both requirements document and to-do list
learnings.detail: Each user story in prd.json carries a passes flag telling the LLM whether the behavior actually works in the app yet - e.g. 'beats display as three orange ellipses dots below the clip' with verify steps, marked passes true when done. Matt iterates on this file with an LLM, and it represents the entire sprint backlog: an item is complete exactly when its flag flips. At sprint end he deletes progress.txt but keeps the PRD pattern.

learnings.title: progress.txt is the agent's sprint memory - and append is load-bearing
learnings.detail: progress.txt is a free-text log the LLM appends its learnings to as it works - its memory for the sprint, alongside git history. Matt insists on append rather than update: told to 'update', the LLM rewrites the whole file, while append reliably just adds notes at the end. He even prompts it to leave notes for 'the next person' - pointers like which PRD item to pick next.

learnings.title: One feature per iteration, highest priority first
learnings.detail: The prompt instructs: find the highest-priority feature and work only on that feature - Matt added 'highest priority' after noticing the LLM just picked the first list item. Limiting scope prevents the LLM from biting off more than it can chew, because agents degrade as tokens pile into the context window. It also forces careful task sizing: one enormous task among small ones will swallow an iteration whole, so every PRD item must be small - good practice for humans too.

learnings.title: A git commit per loop gives the agent queryable history
learnings.detail: Each iteration ends by committing the PRD update, the progress.txt entry, and the feature work. This is what lets a later iteration (or a human) use git history to see exactly what was done and why, giving the LLM context for its next task. It also isolates failures: if the loop commits bad code and loses its memory, the offending change is a single bisectable commit rather than a mystery.

learnings.title: Feedback loops are what make Ralph produce working code
learnings.detail: To trust overnight output, CI must stay green on every commit: pnpm typecheck and pnpm test run inside the loop. Matt cites Anthropic's 'Effective harnesses for long-running agents' article as the inspiration for the JSON PRD format and progress.txt, and its finding that Claude marks features complete without proper testing - but verifies end-to-end much better when explicitly prompted to test like a human user, e.g. via browser automation. Keep tasks small so context budget remains for that verification.

learnings.title: ralph-once.sh puts a human in the loop for hard features
learnings.detail: A variant with the same prompt runs a single interactive iteration in the terminal instead of looping detached. Matt uses it for difficult features where he wants to steer the LLM constantly - and as the best way to learn Ralph's behavior. He reports feeling more productive steering ralph-once than authoring multi-phase plans, because the loop metaphor (pull task, finish, repeat) matches how work actually flows.

learnings.title: Live demo: Opus 4.5 picks a PRD item, verifies, and ships it
learnings.detail: Running ralph-once.sh with Opus 4.5 on his course video manager, the agent selects beats PRD items 21-27, reasons that without the visual display working the other beat UI items cannot be verified, plans, implements the beat indicator component, immediately runs typecheck and tests, marks passes true, appends a progress note suggesting the next item, commits - and the right-click 'add beat' feature shows three orange dots in the real editor. He was literally editing his video software with a video running.

learnings.title: Invest in the feedback loops, not the orchestration
learnings.detail: Matt's closing advice: with Ralph, you want more tests, higher-quality non-flaky tests, an MCP server that lets the agent explore the running application, and above all types, types, types - the strongest type system you can get (hence TypeScript). The loop itself is trivial; everything of value lives in the verification infrastructure that catches the agent's mistakes before the next iteration builds on them.

key_points: The way to ship code while you sleep is a for loop - not a swarm, mesh, or orchestrator.
16 parallel agents means merge conflicts; one agent means context overflow; one task per fresh context window threads the needle.
A PRD with passes flags is simultaneously a requirements document and the agent's to-do list.
Say append, not update, or the LLM will rewrite your progress log every iteration.
One feature per iteration - LLMs get stupid as context fills up.
A git commit per iteration turns the loop's history into queryable context.
Types, types, types: the loop is trivial, the feedback loops are the product.
Multi-phase plans make you an anal-retentive planner; Ralph makes you a requirements gatherer.
